# Why Opening PHP Directly from File Explorer Doesn't Work

You can open an HTML file directly from your file system and see it rendered in a browser because the file contains static text that the browser interprets as markup. However, opening a `.php` file directly from the address bar or by double-clicking it will not execute any PHP code. Instead, you will see the raw source code: `<?php echo "Hello"; ?>`. This happens because your web server is not running locally to process the request and inject the output into the HTML response.

To view the results of PHP execution on your local machine, you must run a local development server. While modern frameworks like Laravel include built-in servers that simplify this setup for production-like environments, standalone PHP scripts require a traditional PHP runtime environment configured correctly.

## The Architecture of Local Execution

When you load a URL in a browser, the browser sends an HTTP request to a server. If the URL is `http://localhost/`, it expects a server like Apache or Nginx listening on port 80 (or a custom port) to handle the logic. Without this intermediary, the browser has no way of knowing how to process PHP tags.

The most straightforward solution for development is using the built-in PHP development server (`php -S`). This command starts a lightweight HTTP server that runs directly from your installed PHP binaries.

You can start it by running:

```bash
php -S localhost:8000
```

This launches a server listening on port 8000. To access your files, you must provide a document root path. For example, if you have a file named `index.php` in a directory called `public`, you would navigate to:

```text
http://localhost:8000/public/index.php
```

The server reads the file, executes the PHP logic, and sends the resulting HTML back to your browser. This is significantly more efficient than trying to configure Apache or Nginx solely for local testing, as it avoids complex virtual host configurations and security pitfalls associated with running a full web stack locally.

## Handling File Paths and Directory Structures

A common pitfall when switching from static files to dynamic PHP is how you reference assets like CSS or JavaScript. When using the built-in PHP server (`php -S`), you cannot use relative paths like `/css/style.css`. Because the root of your project is not automatically mapped to `localhost`, those requests fail with 404 errors.

Instead, you must use absolute URLs that match the structure of your project:

```php
<link rel="stylesheet" href="/public/css/style.css">
```

This ensures the browser requests the file relative to the document root defined when starting the server. If you are using a framework like Laravel, the `php artisan serve` command automatically configures this behavior so that routes map directly to your application entry point without needing manual path adjustments.

## Security Considerations for Local Development

Running PHP files locally is safe provided you do not expose your local development environment to the public internet. The primary risk in local development involves accidentally exposing sensitive data or misconfiguring permissions, but this is distinct from the issue of simply running the code.

Unlike production servers where security headers and strict configuration are mandatory, local environments often run with relaxed settings for convenience. For instance, error reporting might be set to `display_errors` instead of logging, which can leak stack traces containing database credentials or file paths into your browser console. Always ensure that `error_reporting` is set appropriately in your `php.ini` or local configuration files before deploying code to production.

## Conclusion

Running PHP files on your local computer requires a server environment, not just the PHP runtime. Using the built-in PHP server (`php -S`) provides a quick and effective way to test scripts without installing complex web server stacks. Just remember to use absolute paths for assets and be mindful of error reporting settings to prevent accidental data leaks during development.
